title: The resurrection of the flesh depends on Christ's true flesh
english: Those who want to unsettle the faith in the resurrection—which before these near relatives of the Sadducees remained without controversy—by denying that this hope extends to the flesh, quite logically tear apart the flesh of Christ with their questions. They claim it was either nothing at all or somehow other than human, because if it is established that it was human, the case is already decided against them: whatever rose in Christ must rise in every way. So the very point from which they destroy the claims of the flesh is where the defenses must be built up for us. Let us examine the bodily substance of the Lord; about the spiritual substance there is no dispute. The flesh is what is in question. Its truth and its quality are being reconsidered: whether it existed, and from where, and of what kind it was. The report of it will give the law for our resurrection. Marcion, in order to deny the flesh of Christ, denied also his birth—or in order to deny his birth, denied his flesh. Naturally, he did not want birth and flesh to testify for each other, since there is no birth without flesh and no flesh without birth. As if he himself could not, with the same heretical license, have either admitted the flesh and denied the birth, as Apelles did—his disciple and later his deserter—or confessed both the flesh and the birth and interpreted them differently, as Valentinus did, his fellow disciple and fellow deserter. But even the man who introduced a supposed flesh of Christ could equally have fabricated the birth as a phantom, so that the conception, the pregnancy, the delivery of the virgin, and the whole course of the infant's life from then on would be held by seeming. They would have deceived the same eyes and the same senses that the supposition of flesh deceived.
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by stating that those who deny the resurrection of the flesh also attack the reality of Christ's flesh, and he will now examine the bodily substance of the Lord.

title: Marcion's deletion of the birth-narratives
english: Gabriel announces the birth. What has his Christ to do with the Creator's angel? And the conception is brought into the virgin's womb. What has he to do with Isaiah, the Creator's prophet? Marcion hates delays, this man who was suddenly bringing Christ down from heaven. "Take away," he says, "those censuses of Caesar that are always such a nuisance, and the cramped lodgings, and the filthy rags, and the hard mangers. Let the angelic multitude see to honoring their Lord at night. Let the shepherds keep their cattle instead, and let the magi not weary themselves from afar; I give them back their gold. Let Herod be better too, so that Jeremiah may not boast. But let the infant not be circumcised, so he won't feel pain, and let him not be carried to the temple, so he won't burden his parents with the cost of the offering, and let him not be handed into Simeon's hands, so the old man about to die won't be saddened from then on. Let that old woman be silent too, so she won't bewitch the boy."

With these plans, I think, you dared, Marcion, to destroy all the original records of Christ, so that his flesh would not be proved. On what authority? Tell me. If you are a prophet, foretell something; if you are an apostle, preach publicly; if you are an apostolic man, think with the apostles; if you are merely a Christian, believe what has been handed down; if you are none of these, I would rightly say: die. For you are dead indeed, you who are not a Christian, by not believing what is believed to make Christians, and you are all the more dead the more you are not a Christian. You, having once been one, fell away by cutting away what you had previously believed, as you yourself confess in a certain letter, and your followers do not deny, and our people prove.

Therefore, by cutting away what you believed, you have cut it away no longer believing; yet not because you ceased to believe did you cut it away rightly. On the contrary, by cutting away what you believed, you prove that before you cut it away it was otherwise. What you believed as otherwise, that was what had been handed down. Moreover, what had been handed down was true, as handed down by those whose task it was to hand it down. Therefore, by cutting away what had been handed down, you cut away what was true. You did it with no right.

But I have already used such preliminary arguments more fully against all heresies elsewhere. After those, I now revisit this matter out of abundance, desiring the reason why you thought Christ was not born.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Marcion directly, charging that Marcion cut out all the Gospel accounts of Christ's birth because they proved his flesh was real.

title: God's will and power to be born without change
english: It follows necessarily, since you think you had the right to decide this, that you judged birth either impossible for God or unworthy of him. But nothing is impossible for God except what he does not will. Let us consider, then, whether he willed the birth—because if he willed it, he both could do it and was born. I take the short way. If God had not willed the birth, for whatever reason, he would not have presented himself as a man to be seen. For who, seeing him as a man, would deny that he had been born? So what he had not willed to be, he would not have willed to be seen at all. The mere opinion of anything displeasing is rejected, because it makes no difference whether a thing exists or not, if when it does not exist it is presumed to exist. Of course it matters that what truly does not exist should not suffer a false report. But, you say, his own conscience was enough for him. Let people think he was born if they wanted, since they saw a man. How much more worthy, then, and how much more consistent it would have been for him to have endured human opinion as one truly born, rather than to undergo that same opinion without the birth, to the injury of his own conscience—which you count as confidence—so that, not born, he would endure being thought born against his own conscience? Tell me what was worth so much that Christ, knowing what he was, should present himself as what he was not. You cannot say, "If he had been born and put on man, he would have ceased to be God, losing what he was while becoming what he was not." For there is no danger to God's own state. But, you say, I deny that God was truly turned into man, so as to undergo birth and be embodied in flesh, because one who is without end must also be unchangeable. For to be turned into another thing is the end of the former thing. Conversion therefore does not suit one whom end does not suit. Clearly, the nature of changeable things has this law: they do not remain in what they are turned into, and so by not remaining they perish, losing what they were by being converted. But nothing is equal to God; his nature stands apart from the condition of all things. If, then, the things that stand apart from God—from which God stands apart—lose what they were when they are converted, where will the difference of divinity from other things be, unless it holds the opposite, that is, that God can be turned into all things and still persevere as he is? Otherwise he will be equal to those things which, when converted, lose what they were—and since he is not equal to them in all things, neither is he in the outcome of conversion. You have read at some time that the Creator's angels were turned into human appearance, and you believed it, and that they carried such truth of body that Abraham washed their feet (Genesis 18:4), and Lot was rescued from the Sodomites by their hands (Genesis 19:16), and an angel also wrestled with a man and desired to be released with the whole weight of his body, so firmly was he held (Genesis 32:24-26). What was permitted to the lower angels of God—to be converted into human bodily form and yet remain angels—will you take away from the more powerful God, as if Christ, truly clothed in man, could not have persevered as God? Or did those angels also appear as phantoms of flesh? But you will not dare to say this. For if in your view the Creator's angels are as Christ is, then Christ will belong to that God whose angels are such as Christ is. If you had not deliberately rejected some Scriptures that resist your opinion and corrupted others, the Gospel of John would have confounded you on this point, preaching that the Spirit in bodily form of a dove descended and settled upon the Lord (John 1:32). That Spirit, since it was this, was as truly a dove as it was the Spirit, and it had not destroyed its own substance by taking on an external substance. But you ask where the body of the dove is, once the Spirit was taken back into heaven—and likewise the bodies of the angels. It was withdrawn by the same means by which it had been produced. If you had seen it when it was brought forth from nothing, you would know also when it was withdrawn into nothing. If its beginning was not visible, neither was its end. Yet the body had solidity, at whatever moment the body was seen. What is written cannot not have been.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Marcion's objection that birth was impossible or unworthy for God, arguing that God could be born and remain God.

title: If birth is not impossible or dangerous for God, Marcion must still call it shameful—but Christ loved the very man born in filth and redeemed him
english: So if you do not reject the taking of a body as impossible for God or as dangerous for him, it remains for you to reject it as unworthy and to accuse it. Begin with birth itself, then—go on, plead your case: the filths of the genital elements in the womb, the foul clots of moisture and blood, the flesh to be nourished from the same mire through nine months. Describe the womb growing swollen day by day, heavy, anxious, not even safe in sleep, uncertain in the cravings and aversions. Attack now also the very modesty of the woman giving birth—a modesty to be honored for its danger, or to be revered for its nature. You shudder, of course, at the infant poured forth with all its burdens, and of course you scorn it once it is washed, because it is bound in swaddling cloths, because it is shaped by anointings, because it is laughed at with caresses. This veneration of nature, Marcion, you spit on—and how were you born? You hate the newborn man, and how do you love anyone? You certainly did not love yourself when you withdrew from the church and the faith of Christ. But that is your concern, if you displease yourself or if you were born otherwise. Certainly Christ loved that man coagulated in the uncleannesses of the womb, that man brought forth through the shameful parts, that man nourished through mockeries. For him he descended, for him he preached, for him he cast himself down in all humility even to death, even death on a cross. He loved, surely, the one whom he redeemed at great cost. If Christ belongs to the Creator, he loved his own, as he deserved; but if he is from another god, he loved him all the more, since he redeemed what was alien. He loved, then, along with the man, also his birth, also his flesh. Nothing can be loved without that through which it is what it is. Either take away birth and produce a man, or take away flesh and present the one whom God redeemed—if these are the man whom God redeemed. Do you make shameful and unworthy for him the very things he redeemed, which he would not have redeemed if he had not loved them? He reforms birth from death by heavenly regeneration, he restores flesh from every affliction, he cleanses the leprous, gives light again to the blind, makes the paralytic whole, purges the demon-possessed, raises the dead—and we are ashamed of that flesh? If he had truly wished to come forth from a wolf or a sow or a cow, and clothed in the body of a wild beast or a herd animal had preached the kingdom of heaven, your judgment, I suppose, would prescribe to him: This is shameful for God, and unworthy of the Son of God, and foolish. Because that is what you believe—and it would indeed be foolish if we were to judge God by our own sense. But look around, Marcion, if you have not erased it: God chose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom. What are these foolish things? The conversion of men to the worship of the true God, the rejection of error, the discipline of justice, chastity, mercy, patience, all innocence? These are not foolish. Ask, then, what he meant; and if you presume to have found it, will it be as foolish as believing in a God who was born—and born of a virgin, and fleshly at that—who rolled about through those insults to nature? Someone may say these things are not foolish, and that there are other things which God chose to rival worldly wisdom. And yet among that wisdom it is more easily believed that Jupiter became a bull or a swan than that Christ was truly a man, according to Marcion.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Marcion directly, pressing the objection that the incarnation is unworthy of God after having already set aside the claims that it was impossible or dangerous.

title: The Folly of a Crucified and Risen God
english: There are plainly other foolish things too, the ones that belong to the insults and passions of God. Or let them call a crucified God wisdom. Take this away too, Marcion—or rather, take this above all. For what is more unworthy of God, what more shameful: to be born or to die? To carry flesh or a cross? To be circumcised or nailed up? To be brought up or buried? To be laid in a manger or shut in a tomb? You will be wiser if you do not believe these things either. But you will not be wise unless you become a fool in the world by believing God's foolish things. Was it for this reason that you did not cut the passions away from Christ, because as a phantom he lacked any sense of them? We said before that he could equally have undergone the empty mockeries of an imaginary birth and infancy. But answer now, killer of truth: was not God truly crucified? Did he not truly die, because he was truly crucified? Was he not truly raised again, because he truly died? Did Paul falsely set himself to know nothing among us but Jesus crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2)? Did he falsely assert that he was buried, falsely insist that he was raised again (1 Corinthians 15:4)? Then our faith is false too, and everything we hope from Christ will be a phantom. You are the wickedest of men, who excuse the killers of God. For Christ suffered nothing from them if he truly suffered nothing. Spare the one hope of the whole world, you who destroy the necessary shame of faith. Whatever is unworthy of God is for my benefit. I am saved if I am not ashamed of my Lord. Whoever is ashamed of me, he says, I will be ashamed of him too (Mark 8:38). I find no other materials for shame that prove me, through contempt of blushing, well shameless and happily foolish. The Son of God was crucified; I am not ashamed, because it is shameful. And the Son of God died; it is entirely believable, because it is absurd. And he was buried and rose again; it is certain, because it is impossible. For how will these things be true in him if he himself was not true, if he did not truly have in himself what could be fastened, what could die, what could be buried and raised again—this flesh, suffused with blood, built on bones, woven with sinews, entwined with veins, which knows how to be born and to die? Human without doubt, as born from a human. And therefore it will be mortal in Christ, because Christ is man and Son of Man. Or why is Christ man and son of man, if he has nothing of man and nothing from man? Unless either man is something other than flesh, or man's flesh comes from somewhere other than man, or Mary is something other than man, or the God of Marcion is man. Otherwise Christ would not be called man without flesh, nor son of man without some human parent, just as he would not be God without the Spirit of God, nor Son of God without God the Father. Thus the census of both substances exhibited him as man and God: born from here, unborn from there; fleshly from here, spiritual from there; weak from here, supremely strong from there; dying from here, living from there. This property of the conditions, divine and human, is marked out by the equal truth of each nature, by the same faith of both spirit and flesh. The powers of the Spirit of God proved him God; the passions proved the flesh of man. If the powers were not without the Spirit, likewise the passions were not without flesh. If the flesh with its passions was feigned, then the Spirit with its powers was false too. Why do you halve Christ with a lie? He was entirely truth. He preferred, believe me, to be born than to lie in any part—and indeed against himself—by carrying flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles, bloody without blood, clothed without a tunic, hungry without hunger, eating without teeth, speaking without a tongue, so that his speech was a phantom to the ears through the image of a voice. Then he was a phantom even after the resurrection, when he offered his hands and feet to his disciples to inspect, saying, Look, that it is I, for a spirit does not have bones as you see me having (Luke 24:39)—without doubt hands and feet and bones, which a spirit does not have, but flesh does. How do you interpret this voice, Marcion, who bring Jesus only from a God who is best and simple and good? Look, he deceives and tricks and cheats the eyes of all, the senses of all, the approaches and touches of all. Then you should have brought Christ not from heaven but from some circus troupe, not God above man but a man magician, not the high priest of salvation but the artisan of spectacle, not the raiser of the dead but the caller away of the living. Except that even if he was a magician, he was born.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Marcion's objection that birth and flesh are unworthy of God, and now turns to the even more shameful things God underwent: death, burial, and crucifixion.

title: Unborn Flesh Cannot Die
english: But some disciples of that Pontic master, driven to seem wiser than their teacher, grant Christ the truth of the flesh, yet without giving up their denial of his birth. He had flesh, they say, but wholly unborn. So we have come, as the saying goes, from lime pit into coal pit, from Marcion to Apelles. After falling in the flesh into a woman and breaking with the school of Marcion, Apelles was then turned in spirit toward the virgin Philumene, and he took up preaching from her the solid body of Christ, but without birth. To that angel of Philumene the apostle will answer with the same voice with which he already then foretold him, saying, "Even if an angel from heaven proclaims to you a different gospel than the one we proclaimed to you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8). Against their further arguments we will make our stand.

They admit that Christ truly had a body. Then where does its matter come from, if not from the condition in which it appeared? Where does a body come from, if a body is not flesh? Where does flesh come from, if it was not born? For whatever is destined to be born must be born. From the stars, they say, and from substances of the upper world he borrowed flesh. And they insist there is nothing strange in a body without birth, since even among us angels were able to proceed into flesh with no work of a womb. We grant that Scripture reports this. But how can the faith of one rule borrow the weapon for its own arguments from the very faith it attacks? What has he to do with Moses, when he has rejected the God of Moses? If his god is another, let that god's realities be otherwise. Still, let all heretics use the Scriptures of the one whose world they also use. This too will stand as testimony of judgment against them, that they build their blasphemies out of his own examples. It is easy for the truth to win, even when it enters no such plea against them.

So let those who cite the angels as the pattern for the flesh of Christ, calling it unborn though flesh, compare the reasons why Christ and why the angels proceeded into flesh. No angel ever came down to be crucified, to undergo death, to be raised from death. If the angels' taking of bodies never had such a cause, you have the reason why they received flesh without birth. They had not come to die, and so they had not come to be born. But Christ, sent to die, had also to be born of necessity, so that he could die. For commonly only what is born dies. Birth has a mutual debt with mortality. The shape of dying is the cause of birth. If Christ died on account of what dies, and what dies is what is also born, it followed, indeed it came first, that he should equally be born on account of what is born, because he had to die on account of the very thing which dies because it is born. It did not fit him to remain unborn for the sake of that for which it fitted him to die. Yet even then, among those angels, the Lord himself appeared to Abraham without birth, with flesh of course, for the same difference of cause. But you do not accept this, since you do not accept Christ, who even then was learning to address and free and judge the human race in the garb of flesh not yet born, because not yet to die, until his birth and his mortality were first announced. Let them then prove that those angels drew flesh from the stars. If they cannot prove it, because it is not written, then the flesh of Christ will not come from there either, though they fit the angels to him as an example.

It is agreed that the angels bore flesh not their own, since by nature they are of spiritual substance, though of some body of their own kind, yet able for a time to appear transformed into flesh and to meet with men. Since Scripture does not report where they took flesh from, our understanding is left with no doubt that this belongs to angelic power, to take to itself a body from no matter. How much more readily, you ask, from some matter? That is certain. But nothing is settled on this point, because Scripture shows nothing. Moreover, if they can make themselves what by nature they are not, why can they not make from no substance? If they become what they are not, why should they not become from what is not? And what is not, when it comes to be, is from nothing. So Scripture neither asks nor shows what afterward became of those bodies. What was from nothing became nothing. Those who could turn themselves into flesh can turn nothing itself into flesh. It is greater to change nature than to make matter. But even if the angels had to take flesh from matter, it is surely more credible that they took it from earthly matter than from any kind of heavenly substances, since their flesh proved of so earthly a quality that it fed on earthly foods. Suppose it was starry, and even now starry, fed in the same way on earthly foods though it would not be earthly, just as what was earthly fed on heavenly foods though it would not be heavenly, for we read that manna was given to the people for food: "Man ate the bread of angels" (Psalm 78:25). Still, the condition of the Lord's flesh, once set apart, is not broken by the cause of a different arrangement. Since he was to be truly man even unto death, he had to put on that flesh whose mark is death. And birth comes before that flesh whose mark is death.
orientation: Apelles once a follower of Marcion claims Christ had real flesh borrowed from starry things without birth like angels and Tertullian answers why birth was needed for death.

title: The announcement of mother and brothers was a test, not a denial of birth
english: But whenever the question of birth is raised, all who reject it as prejudging the truth of the flesh in Christ want to deny that God himself was born, because he said, “Who is mother to me, and who are brothers to me?” (Matthew 12:48). So let Apelles also hear what I have already answered to Marcion in that book in which I challenged his own gospel: the context of that announcement must be considered.

First of all, no one would ever have announced to him that his mother and brothers were standing outside unless he was certain that he had a mother and brothers, and that these were the very people he was announcing—either known to him before or discovered then and there. Though these heresies have cut this passage out of the gospel for that very reason, because those who marveled at his teaching were saying that his supposed father Joseph the carpenter, his mother Mary, and his brothers and sisters were very well known to them.

But, you say, they announced his mother and brothers to him for the sake of testing him, whom he did not have. Scripture does not say this, though elsewhere it does not keep silent when something was done to test him. “Look,” it says, “a teacher of the law stood up to test him” (Luke 10:25). And elsewhere, “The Pharisees came to him to test him” (Matthew 19:3). Nothing prevented it from also being stated here that this was done in order to test him. But I do not accept what you bring in from outside Scripture.

Next, there must be a reason for the testing. What did they think they were testing in him? Surely whether he had been born or not. For if his answer denied it, the announcement of the testers was aiming at that. But no test that aims at discovering something about a person it doubts proceeds so abruptly that a question does not come first—a question that introduces the doubt and prompts the test.

Furthermore, if the question of Christ's birth was never discussed anywhere, why do you argue that they wanted to find out through a test what they never brought into question? I add this too: even if he had to be tested about his birth, he would not have been tested in this way, by announcing persons who might not have existed even if Christ had been born. We are all born, and yet not all of us have brothers or a mother. A man can have a father rather than a mother, and uncles rather than brothers. So a test about birth does not fit here, since birth could be established without naming a mother or brothers.

It is far more plausible that, being certain he had a mother and brothers, they were testing his divinity rather than his birth—whether he knew what was outside while he was inside, when they falsely announced the presence of people who were not present. Except that this would have made the test pointless. For it could have happened that the people they announced as standing outside were known to him to be away, kept away by illness, business, or travel. No one tests in a way that he knows could bring him the shame of a failed test.

Since no reason for testing fits, the plain meaning of the announcement stands: his mother and brothers had truly come. But let Apelles also learn the reason for the answer of the one who denied his mother and brothers at that moment. The Lord's brothers had not believed in him, as is contained in the gospel published before Marcion. Likewise his mother is not shown to have stayed close to him, while other women—Martha and Mary—are found in his company.

In this passage their unbelief is finally apparent. While Jesus was teaching the way of life, while he was preaching the kingdom of God, while he was working to heal sicknesses and defects, with strangers fixed on him, those so close to him were absent. Finally they arrive and stand outside, and do not enter—evidently not considering what was happening inside. They do not even wait, as if they were bringing something necessary to what he was doing at that very moment, but they interrupt and want to call him away from so great a work.

Tell me, Apelles—or you, Marcion—if you were playing a board game or competing about actors or charioteers and were called away by such an announcement, would you not have said, “Who is mother to me, or who are brothers?” Christ was preaching and proving God, fulfilling the law and the prophets, scattering the darkness of so long an age—was it unworthy of him to use this saying to strike the unbelief of those standing outside, or to shake off the importunity of those calling him away from his work?

Besides, to deny his birth there would have been another place, another time, another order of speech—not a saying that could also be spoken by someone who did have a mother and brothers. When indignation denies parents, it does not deny them; it rebukes them. Finally, he made others more important, and by showing the ground of his preference—namely, hearing the word—he shows on what condition he denied mother and brothers. For by the very thing by which he adopted others who clung to him, he disowned those who stood apart from him.

Christ also usually fulfills what he teaches others. What kind of example would it be if, while teaching that mother or father or brothers are not to be valued as highly as the Word, he himself, when his mother and brothers were announced, abandoned the Word? So he denied his parents in the way he taught they must be denied for the work of God.

But there is also another meaning: the mother set apart is a figure of the synagogue, and the unbelieving brothers a figure of the Jews. In them Israel was outside, but the new disciples inside, hearing and believing and clinging to Christ, were sketching out the church—which he called a more excellent mother and a worthier brotherhood, rejecting the fleshly family. In the same sense he answered that exclamation too, not denying his mother's womb and breasts, but declaring more blessed those who hear the Word (Luke 11:28).
orientation: Tertullian is answering Apelles and Marcion, who use Christ's words 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?' to deny that Christ was truly born.

title: The starry flesh of Apelles is still flesh of sin
english: These are the only passages on which Marcion and Apelles think they have the strongest support. Once they are interpreted according to the truth of the whole and uncorrupted Gospel, that should have been enough to prove human flesh in Christ by defending his birth. But since these followers of Apelles especially hold up the disgrace of the flesh—which they claim was built into souls seduced by that fiery ruler of evil, and therefore unworthy of Christ, and therefore a substance from the stars befitted him—I must strike them back with their own equipment.

They name a certain glorious angel who established this world and, after establishing it, admitted repentance. We have treated this in its proper place. For we also have a little book against them, asking whether one who had the Spirit and will and power of Christ for those works did anything worthy of repentance, since they even interpret the angel as a figure of the wandering sheep.

So by the testimony of its founder's repentance, the world will be sin, since all repentance is a confession of sin, because it has no place except in sin. If the world is sin, as body and members, then the sky and the heavenly things will likewise be sin and whatever is conceived and brought forth from there. And a bad tree must produce bad fruit.

Therefore Christ's flesh, built from heavenly things, consists of the elements of sin—sinful from a sinful stock—and it will already be part of that substance, namely ours, which they refuse to attribute to Christ as sinful. So if there is no difference in disgrace, either let them devise some material of purer mark for Christ, since ours displeases them, or let them acknowledge the same material, since even a heavenly one could not be better.

We certainly read: The first man was from the mud of the earth, the second man from heaven (1 Corinthians 15:47). But this does not look to a difference of material; rather, to the earthly substance of the first man's flesh—that is, Adam's—it opposes the heavenly substance from the Spirit of the second man, that is, Christ. And he refers the heavenly man to the Spirit, not to the flesh, so much so that those he compares to him are clearly made heavenly in this earthly flesh, by the Spirit of course.

For if Christ were heavenly according to the flesh as well, those who are not heavenly according to the flesh would not be compared to him. If therefore those who become heavenly—as Christ also is—bear the earthly substance of flesh, this also confirms that Christ himself was heavenly in earthly flesh, just as those are who are made equal to him.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Apelles and his followers, who say Christ's flesh was made of starry substance because ordinary flesh is unworthy of him.

title: The earthly signs of Christ's flesh
english: We maintain further that nothing taken from something else can be so different from its source that it gives no hint of where it came from. No material lacks testimony to its origin, even if it is changed into a new character. Our own body, certainly—the one formed from clay, which truth has handed down even to the myths of the nations—confesses the origin of both elements: flesh from earth, blood from water. For although the appearance of its quality is different, this is what happens when one thing becomes another from something else. After all, what is blood but red liquid? What is flesh but earth in its own shape? Consider each quality: muscles like clods, bones like rocks, even little stones around the nipples. Look at the tight connections of sinews like runners of roots, and the branching courses of veins like windings of streams, and the downy hairs like moss, and the hair like turf, and the hidden treasures of the marrow themselves like the ores of the flesh. All these signs of earthly origin were in Christ and still are; they hid him as the Son of God, so that he was regarded as a man for no other reason than that he displayed the substance of a human body. Or produce something heavenly in him, begged from the Bears, the Pleiades and the Hyades. For the things we have listed are as much evidence of earthly flesh as our own. But I find nothing new, nothing foreign. In fact, it was only by his words and deeds, his teaching and power alone, that people were astonished at Christ as a man. If there had been any novelty in his flesh, it would have been noted and considered a miracle. But the unremarkable condition of his earthly flesh was itself what made the rest of him remarkable, when they said, "Where did this man get this teaching and these signs?" (Mark 6:2). Even those who despised his appearance spoke this way. So his body did not even possess human beauty, much less heavenly glory. Even if the prophets among us are silent about his ignoble appearance, his very sufferings and insults speak. The sufferings proved human flesh; the insults proved it was dishonorable. Would anyone have dared to graze a new body with the tip of a fingernail, or defile its face with spittle, unless it deserved it? You call his flesh heavenly, but you have no reason to understand it as heavenly. Why do you deny it is earthly, when you have reason to recognize it as earthly? He hungered under the devil, thirsted with the Samaritan woman, wept over Lazarus, trembled at death—"For the flesh," he says, "is weak" (Matthew 26:41)—and finally shed his blood. These are, I think, heavenly signs. But how, I ask, could he have been despised and suffered, as I have already said, if anything of heavenly nobility had shone in that flesh? From this, then, we prove that nothing in it came from heaven, precisely so that it could be despised and suffer.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's body was ordinary earthly flesh, and here he lists the physical features and experiences that prove it was not heavenly.

title: Against the view that Christ's flesh was made of soul
english: I turn now to others who are equally wise in their own eyes: those who claim that Christ's flesh was made of soul, because the soul became flesh, and therefore the flesh became soul, and just as the flesh was made of soul, so the soul was fleshly. Here too I ask for their reasons. If Christ took up a soul into himself in order to make the soul safe, because it could not be made safe except through him while it was in him, I do not see why by putting on flesh he made it flesh made of soul, as if he could not make the soul safe in any other way unless it became flesh. For since he makes our souls safe even though they are not only not fleshly but also separated from flesh, how much more could he have brought that soul which he himself took up to safety even without making it fleshly? Again, since they presume that Christ came for the purpose of freeing not our flesh but our soul alone, first, how absurd it is that he who was going to free the soul alone made it into the kind of body he was not going to free. Then, if he had undertaken to free our souls through that soul which he bore, he ought to have borne a soul like ours as well—that is, of our form, whatever form our soul has in its hidden state, but certainly not fleshly. Otherwise he did not free our soul, if the soul he had was fleshly; for ours is not fleshly. Further, if he did not free our soul because he freed a fleshly one, that has nothing to do with us, because he did not free our soul. But neither did a soul that was not ours need to be freed—that is, a fleshly one. For it was not in danger if it was not ours, that is, not fleshly. But it is agreed that it was freed. Therefore it was not fleshly, and it was ours, if it was the soul that was freed, since it was in danger. Now then, if the soul in Christ was not fleshly, neither could the flesh have been made of soul.
orientation: Tertullian has just argued that Christ's flesh was earthly, not heavenly; now he turns to those who say Christ's flesh was made of soul, and asks why Christ would have made the soul flesh if he came to save the soul.

title: Refuting the claim that Christ's soul was made visible by becoming flesh
english: But let us meet them on another argument, demanding why Christ, by taking on flesh made of soul, should be thought to have had a fleshly soul. For God, they say, eagerly desired to display a visible soul to human beings by making it a body—a soul that had previously been invisible, seeing nothing by nature, not even itself, because of the hindrance of this flesh, so that it was even debated whether the soul had been born or not. And so the soul was made a body in Christ, so that we might see it being born, dying, and—what is more—rising again. But what sort of thing was this, that the soul should be demonstrated through flesh to itself or to us, when it could not be recognized through flesh, and so it was shown by becoming the very thing in which it lay hidden—that is, flesh? It took on darkness, apparently, so that it could shine. Let us first reconsider, then, whether the soul ought to have been displayed in this way, and then whether they claim it was entirely invisible before—whether as incorporeal, or as having some kind of body of its own. And yet when they call it invisible, they make it corporeal, since it has something that is invisible. For how can something be called invisible if it has nothing invisible? But it cannot even exist unless it has something through which it exists. And since it exists, it must have something through which it exists. If it has something through which it exists, that will be its body. Everything that exists is a body of its own kind. Nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist. Therefore, since the soul has an invisible body, the one who undertook to make it visible would surely have done better to make visible that part of it which was invisible, because neither falsehood nor weakness befits God—falsehood, if he displayed the soul as something other than it was; weakness, if he was unable to display what it was. No one who wants to show a man puts a helmet or a mask on him. But this is what happened to the soul, if, changed in flesh, it put on a foreign surface. But even if the soul is considered incorporeal, so that by some force of reason the soul is indeed hidden, yet whatever the soul is, it is not a body—still, it would not have been impossible for God, and it would have suited his purpose more fittingly, to display it in some new kind of body rather than in this common one shared by all, which was already known, lest he should have eagerly desired without cause to make the soul visible from invisible, exposed, of course, to these very questions by the laying of human flesh as a covering upon it. But Christ could not be seen among human beings except as a man. Give back therefore to Christ the faith that is his: that he who chose to walk as a man also displayed a soul of human condition, not making it fleshly, but clothing it in flesh.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the view of Apelles and his followers that Christ took a soul-made body so that the previously invisible soul could be seen.

title: The soul's self-knowledge and what Christ revealed
english: Now let the soul be displayed through flesh, if it has been established that it had to be displayed in some way—that is, as something unknown to itself and to us. Though in this matter the distinction is an empty one, as if we existed apart from the soul, when everything we are is soul. Without soul we are nothing—not even the name of man, but of corpse. If we do not know the soul, then the soul does not know itself. So the only thing left to examine is whether the soul was ignorant of itself here, so that it might become known in some way.

In my opinion, the soul's nature is capable of sensation. No animal is without sensation, and nothing capable of sensation is without soul. To put it more forcefully, sensation is the soul of the soul. Since the soul grants sensation to all things, and itself perceives the sensations of all things—not to mention their qualities—is it likely that it did not receive from the beginning a perception of itself? How would it know what is sometimes necessary for it, by the necessity of natural things, if it does not know its own quality, to which something is necessary? This can be recognized in every soul—I mean self-knowledge—and without this self-knowledge no soul could have served itself.

But I think it belongs more to man, the only rational animal, to have received a soul that makes him a rational animal, the soul itself being rational in the first place. How can it be rational, when it makes man a rational animal, if it does not know its own rationality, being ignorant of itself? But it is so far from ignorant that it knows its maker, its judge, and its condition. Though it has learned nothing yet about God, it names God, and though admitting nothing yet about his judgment, it commends itself to God. Hearing above all that there is no hope after death, it invokes a blessing or a curse on each one who has died well or badly. The little book I wrote, On the Testimony of the Soul, pursues these matters more fully.

Otherwise, if the soul had been ignorant of itself from the beginning, it ought to have learned nothing from Christ except what it was. But in fact it did not learn its form from Christ, but its salvation. The Son of God descended and took on a soul, not so that the soul might know itself in Christ, but so that it might know Christ in itself. For it is not endangered in its salvation by not knowing itself, but by not knowing the Word. Life, he says, was made manifest—not the soul. And I came, he says, to save the soul—he did not say to display it.

We were ignorant, of course, that the soul, though invisible, is born and dies, unless it were exhibited bodily. We were plainly ignorant that it would rise again with the flesh. This is what Christ made manifest. But he did this no differently in himself than in some Lazarus, whose flesh was not animal, just as his soul was not fleshly. What more, then, has been revealed to us about the previously unknown condition of the soul? What invisible aspect of it was there that desired visibility through flesh?
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's soul was shown through his flesh, and now examines whether the soul was unknown to itself and to us, and what Christ actually revealed about the soul.

title: If soul became flesh, the two names and substances collapse
english: The soul, they say, was made flesh so that the soul might be shown. Was the flesh, then, also made soul so that the flesh might be revealed? If the soul is flesh, it is no longer soul but flesh. If the flesh is soul, it is no longer flesh but soul. Where, then, is flesh, and where is soul? Each has become the other. No, if they are neither, while each becomes the other, it is certainly most perverse that when we name flesh we should understand soul, and when we mean soul we should interpret it as flesh. Everything will be in danger of being taken otherwise than it is, and of losing what it is while it is taken otherwise, if it is called otherwise than it is. The faithfulness of names is the safety of properties. Even when qualities are changed, they take possession of the words. For example, clay baked out takes the name of potsherd. It does not share in the name of its former kind, because it does not share in the kind itself. So also the soul of Christ, made flesh, cannot not be what it was made, and cannot be what it was, since it was made something else. And since we have brought in this example, let us use it more fully. Certainly a potsherd from clay is one body and one name, of one body. It cannot be called both potsherd and clay, because what it was, it is not, and what it is not, does not cling to it. And the soul does not cling. Therefore the soul made flesh is a uniform solidity and a total singleness and an undivided substance. But in Christ we find soul and flesh set forth with simple and bare words, that is, soul as soul and flesh as flesh, nowhere soul as flesh or flesh as soul, when they should have been so named if they had been so, but each substance is also pronounced separately by him, for the distinction of the two qualities, soul apart and flesh apart. What then? "My soul is anxious even to death," he says (Matthew 26:38), and "The bread that I will give for the salvation of the world is my flesh" (John 6:51). But if the soul had been flesh, there would be one thing in Christ: a fleshly soul or flesh made of soul. But when he divides the kinds, flesh and soul, he shows two. If two, then not one; if not one, then neither a fleshly soul nor flesh made of soul. For soul-flesh or flesh-soul is one thing. Unless he was bearing another soul besides the one that was flesh, and carrying around another flesh besides the one that was soul. But if there is one flesh and one soul, the one anxious even to death and the one bread for the salvation of the world, the number of two substances distinct in their kind is safe, excluding the single species of a fleshly soul.
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the view that Christ's flesh was made of soul, arguing from the logic of names and substances that soul and flesh must remain two distinct things in Christ.

title: Christ did not bear an angel
english: But they say Christ bore an angel. On what ground? On the same ground on which he bore a man. Then the reason for Christ bearing a man is the same. The salvation of man was the reason—to restore what had perished. Man had perished; man had to be restored. For Christ to bear an angel, there is no such reason. For even if destruction is reckoned to the angels, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels, restoration has never been promised to them. Christ received no command from the Father about the salvation of angels. What the Father neither promised nor commanded, Christ could not carry out. So for what purpose did he bear an angel too, except as a strong attendant, with whom he might work out the salvation of man? For the Son of God was not sufficient, alone, to free man, who had been cast down by a single, solitary serpent. Then there is no longer one God, nor one savior, if there are two artificers of salvation, and each one needing the other. Or was it so that he might free man through an angel? Why then did he descend to do what he was going to accomplish through an angel? If through an angel, why did he himself come? If through himself, why the angel?

He was indeed called the angel of great counsel, that is, a messenger—a title of office, not of nature. For he was going to announce to the world the great plan of the Father, namely the restoration of man. But he is not therefore to be understood as an angel like some Gabriel or Michael. For the son is also sent to the vine-dressers by the lord of the vineyard, just as the servants were, to seek the fruits. But the son will not for that reason be counted as one of the servants, because he took up the servants' office. So I would more readily say, if anything, that the Son himself is an angel—that is, a messenger of the Father—than that an angel was in the Son.

But since it was declared about the Son himself: "You have diminished him a little below the angels" (Psalm 8:5), how will he be seen to have put on an angel, when he is diminished below the angels in this way—as he becomes man, as flesh and soul and Son of Man? But as the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High, can he be held below the angels—he who is God and the Son of God? Therefore, as much as he was made lower than the angels while bearing a man, so much was he not made lower while bearing an angel.

This opinion could suit Ebion, who made Jesus a bare man, solely from the seed of David—that is, not also the Son of God—though clearly somewhat more glorious than the prophets, so that he might declare that an angel was in him, just as in Zechariah. Except that Christ never said: "And the angel who was speaking in me said to me." Nor did he use that daily formula of all the prophets: "Thus says the Lord." For he himself was the Lord, speaking openly from his own authority: "But I say to you" (Matthew 5:22). What more is there to say? Hear Isaiah crying out: "Not an angel, nor a legate, but the Lord himself saved them" (Isaiah 63:9).
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the view that Christ bore an angel, after having argued that Christ bore true human flesh and soul.

title: The heretics' privilege of inventing Christ's flesh
english: Valentinus too enjoyed the heretic's privilege of inventing a spiritual flesh for Christ. Anyone who refused to believe that flesh was human could make it into whatever he pleased. For if it was not human and not from a human being—and this applies to all of them—I do not see from what substance Christ could have declared himself to be a man and the Son of Man: “But now you are trying to kill a man who has told you the truth” (John 8:40), and “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath” (Matthew 12:8). Isaiah says of him: “A man of suffering, and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). And Jeremiah: “He is a man, and who has known him?” (Jeremiah 17:9). And Daniel: “And on the clouds, like a Son of Man” (Daniel 7:13). The apostle Paul too: “The mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Likewise Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus of Nazareth, a man sent to you by God” (Acts 2:22)—certainly a man.

These alone should have been enough, in place of a formal objection, to testify that his flesh was human, taken from a human being, and not spiritual—just as it was not made of soul, nor starry, nor imaginary—if heresies could exist without the zeal and cunning of contention. For instance, as I have read in the work of someone from Valentinus's little faction, they first do not hold that an earthly and human substance was formed for Christ, lest the Lord be found inferior to the angels, who were not made of earthly flesh. Then they say that a flesh like ours ought to be born in the same way—not from the Spirit, nor from God, but from a man's will.

And why not from corruption, but from incorruption? And why is our flesh, equal to his, not immediately taken up, just as his rose and was taken up into heaven? Or why was his flesh, equal to ours, not likewise dissolved into the earth? The heathen used to ponder such things. “So the Son of God was emptied to such a degree of humility?” And: “If he rose as an example for our hope, why has nothing of the kind been proven for us?” The heathen are right to say such things—but so are the heretics. Is there any difference between them, except that the heathen believe by not believing, while the heretics do not believe by believing?

They read, after all: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:5), and they deny the inferior substance of Christ—the one who declared himself not a man but a worm, who had neither form nor beauty; but his form was ignoble, despised beyond all men, a man of suffering, and knowing how to bear weakness (Isaiah 53:2-3). They acknowledge a man mixed with God, and they deny the man. They believe he died, and they contend that what died was born from incorruption—as if corruption were anything other than death.
But our flesh too should have risen immediately. Wait. Christ has not yet crushed his enemies, so that he may triumph over them with his friends.
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the heretical views of Christ's flesh, now turning to Valentinus, who claimed Christ's flesh was spiritual.

title: Alexander's charge that Tertullian says Christ emptied sinful flesh
english: Moreover, that Alexander, out of his heretical cast of mind and love of argument, made room for himself by claiming that we assert Christ put on flesh of earthly estate precisely in order to empty in himself the flesh of sin. Even if we did say this, we would defend our position by whatever reasoning we could—so long as it is not that madness by which he supposed that we regard the very flesh of Christ as sinful and emptied in him, when we remember that it sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven, and we proclaim that it will come from there on the tribunal of the Father's glory. So far are we from being able to call it emptied, that we also cannot call it sinful or emptied, since in it there was no deceit.

But we defend not that the flesh of sin was emptied in Christ, but the sin of the flesh—not the material, but the nature, not the substance, but the fault—according to the authority of the apostle, who says, "He emptied sin in the flesh" (Romans 8:3). For elsewhere he says that Christ was "in the likeness of the flesh of sin" (Romans 8:3), not meaning that he took the likeness of flesh as if it were the image of a body and not the reality, but he wants us to understand the likeness of sinful flesh. For Christ's flesh itself was not sinful, but it was equal to that flesh whose sin was in it—equal in kind, not in the fault of Adam. From this we also confirm that the flesh in Christ was that whose nature is sinful in man, and that in it sin was emptied, because in Christ it is possessed without sin, whereas in man it was not possessed without sin.

For it would not serve Christ's purpose—he who empties the sin of the flesh—not to empty it in that flesh in which the nature of sin existed, nor would it serve his glory. For what great thing is it if he redeemed the blemish of sin in a better flesh of another, that is, of a non-sinful nature? "Therefore," you say, "if he put on our flesh, Christ's flesh was sinful." Do not compress a meaning that can be unfolded. For by putting on our flesh he made it his own; by making it his own he made it free of sin.

As for what should be said to all who think our flesh was not in Christ because it was not from the seed of a man, let them remember that Adam himself was made into this flesh not from the seed of a man. Just as the earth was turned into this flesh without the seed of a man, so also the Word was able to pass into the material of the same flesh without coagulation.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Alexander, who misrepresents him as saying Christ took earthly flesh in order to empty sinful flesh in himself.

title: The New Birth from the Virgin, Prefigured in Adam and Eve
english: But let me dismiss Alexander with his syllogisms, which he twists in his arguments, and also the psalms of Valentinus, which he inserts with great impudence as if they came from some worthy author. Let me direct our engagement to a single line: did Christ receive flesh from the virgin, so that it is established as human in this particular way, if he drew its substance from a human womb? Although it has already become clear from the name of man, from the condition of its qualities, from the sense of its treatment, and from the outcome of its passion that it was human. Before everything, however, I must commend the reason that presided over the Son of God's birth from a virgin. He had to be born in a new way, the inaugurator of a new birth, about which the Lord was proclaimed by Isaiah as the one who would give a sign. What is that sign? "Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son" (Isaiah 7:14). Therefore the virgin conceived and bore Immanuel, God with us. This is the new birth, while man is born in God. In this man God was born, flesh of the ancient seed having been taken up without the ancient seed, so that he might reform it with new seed, that is, spiritually, cleansed with the filth of antiquity excluded. But all this newness, as in everything, was prefigured from the old, by a rational arrangement through a virgin, when the Lord was born as man. The earth was still a virgin, "not yet pressed by work, not yet subdued for sowing; from it we receive man made by God into a living soul" (Genesis 2:7). Therefore if the first Adam is so handed down, rightly the following, or last Adam, as the apostle said, was brought forth by God from the earth, that is, flesh not yet opened for generation, into a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). And yet let me not leave unexamined the intrusion of the name Adam — why Christ was called Adam by the apostle, if his man was not of earthly origin? But here too reason defends it: that God recovered his image and likeness, captured by the devil, by a rival operation. For into the virgin Eve the word that builds death had crept in. Into a virgin equally the Word that builds life had to be introduced, so that what had gone into perdition through this kind of sex might be brought back into salvation through the same sex. Eve had believed the serpent: Mary believed Gabriel. What the former did wrong by believing, the latter wiped out by believing. But Eve then conceived nothing in her womb from the devil's word. No, she conceived. For from then on, so that she might bear as an outcast and bear in pains, the devil's word was seed to her. She brought forth at last a fratricidal devil. Against this, Mary brought forth him who would one day make safe his carnal brother Israel, his own killer. Therefore God brought his Word into the womb, a good brother, to erase the memory of the evil brother. Christ had to come forth for the salvation of man from the place where man, already condemned, had entered.
orientation: Tertullian has set aside Alexander and Valentinus and now argues directly that Christ took flesh from the Virgin, showing that this new birth was fitting and was prefigured in the creation of Adam and the fall of Eve.

title: Why the Son of God took flesh without human seed
english: Now, to answer more simply: it was not fitting for the Son of God to be born from human seed, because if he were entirely Son of Man, he would not also be Son of God, and he would have nothing more than Solomon or Jonah. In that case, he would have to be believed according to Ebion's opinion. Therefore, since he was already the Son of God from the seed of God the Father—that is, the Spirit—the only flesh that suited him, so that he might also be Son of Man, was flesh taken from the flesh of man without a man's seed. A man's seed had no role for one who already had God's seed.

Just as he could have God as Father without a human mother before he was born of the virgin, so when he was born of the virgin he could have a human mother without a human father. In this way he is man with God, since his flesh is the flesh of man with the Spirit of God: flesh without seed from a human being, Spirit with seed from God. If it was the plan of reason that the Son of God should be brought forth from a virgin, why would he not receive from the virgin the body he brought forth from the virgin? Because what he took from God is one thing, they say, since the Word was made flesh (John 1:14).

This phrase testifies what was made flesh, but it is not endangered as if something other than the Word was suddenly made flesh. If the Word was made flesh out of flesh, or if it was made out of seed itself, let Scripture say so. Since Scripture says only what was made, not also from what it was made, it suggests that it was made from something else, not from itself. If not from itself but from something else, then consider from what it is more fitting to believe the Word was made flesh—if not from the flesh in which it was also made. The Lord himself pronounced this as a settled and definitive judgment: What is born of the flesh is flesh (John 3:6), because it is born of flesh.

But if he said this only about man and not about himself, then plainly deny that Christ is man, and in that way defend that it did not apply to him. Yet he adds: And what is born of the Spirit is Spirit (John 3:6)—because God is Spirit (John 4:24), and he is born of God. This certainly points to him all the more, if it also points to those who believe in him. If this applies to him, why not the earlier statement too? You cannot divide it so that this applies to him and the earlier statement applies to other men—not if you do not deny both substances of Christ, flesh and Spirit. Since he had both flesh and Spirit, when he pronounces on the condition of the two substances which he himself bears, he cannot be seen to have determined about his Spirit but not about his flesh. So since he himself is of the Spirit of God and the Spirit is God, he is born of God; and he is of the flesh of man, a man generated in flesh.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that Christ should not have been born of a virgin, by explaining why he took flesh from Mary without a human father.

title: The Flesh Born of God, Not of Human Will
english: What then does it mean, “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but born of God” (John 1:13)? I will rather make use of this passage myself, once I have refuted those who adulterate it. They contend that it was written this way: “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of man, but they were born of God,” as if it designated the believers in his name mentioned above, to show that there is that secret seed of the elect and spiritual ones, which they steep themselves in. But how will that be, when all who believe in the name of the Lord are born of blood and of the will of the flesh and of man, by the common law of the human race—even Valentinus himself? It is written in the singular, as of the Lord: “And he was born of God.” Rightly so, because he is the Word, and with the Word the Spirit, and in the Spirit of God the power, and whatever is of God, Christ is. But as for his flesh, it was not of blood nor of the will of the flesh and of man, because by the will of God the Word became flesh (John 1:14). The denial of our formal birth pertains to the flesh, not to the Word, because the flesh had to be born this way, not the Word.

But when he denied that he was born of the will of the flesh, why did he not also deny that he was of the substance of flesh? For in denying that he was of blood, he did not reject the substance of flesh, but the material of seed, which is known to be the heat of blood, changed by foaming into the coagulation of the blood of the female. For in cheese the curd holds the force of a substance, that is, of milk, which the curdling binds together. We understand therefore that the Lord's birth from intercourse is denied, which the will of man and of the flesh savors of, not from participation in the womb. And why did he so emphatically inculcate that he was not born of blood nor of the will of the flesh or of man, except because it was flesh which no one would doubt was born from intercourse? In denying then that he was from intercourse, he did not deny that he was from flesh; rather, he confirmed that he was from flesh, because he did not deny he was from flesh in the same way as he denied he was from intercourse.

I ask you, if the Spirit of God descended into the womb not about to share flesh from the womb, why did he descend into the womb? For spiritual flesh could have been made outside it; much more simply would it have been made outside the womb than inside the womb. Without cause he brought himself into that from which he took nothing out. But he did not descend into the womb without cause. Therefore he received from it, because if he did not receive from it, he descended into it without cause—especially since he was about to be flesh of a quality which did not belong to the womb, that is, spiritual.
orientation: Tertullian is refuting the Valentinian reading of John 1:13, arguing that the verse's singular 'born of God' refers to Christ alone, and that denying his birth from blood and human will does not deny his birth from Mary's flesh.

title: The grammar of birth: 'in' and 'from' the virgin
english: But how crooked you are! You try to take away the very syllable EX, which is assigned the function of a preposition, and use another one instead, which in this kind of expression is not found in the holy Scriptures. You say he was born through the virgin, not from the virgin, and in the womb, not from the womb, because the angel in a dream said to Joseph: “For what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20), not “from her.” Yet surely, even if he had said “from her,” he had said “in her”; for what was from her was in her. So when he says “in her,” it agrees with “from her,” because what was in her was from her. But it is good that the same Matthew, tracing the origin of the Lord from Abraham down to Mary, says: “Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ is born” (Matthew 1:16). Paul also silences these grammarians. “God,” he says, “sent his Son made from a woman” (Galatians 4:4). Is it “through a woman” or “in a woman”? This is even more emphatic, because he says “made” rather than “born”; he could have said “born” more simply. But by saying “made,” he also confirmed “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14) and asserted the truth of the flesh made from the virgin. The Psalms will also support us in this matter—not the Psalms of the apostate and heretic and Platonist Valentinus, but of the most holy and most received prophet David. He sings among us of Christ, through whom Christ himself sang of himself. Take Christ and hear the Lord speaking to God the Father: “Because you are the one who tore me away from my mother’s womb” (Psalm 22:9). There is one. “And my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb” (Psalm 22:10). There is another. “And from my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 22:10). There is another. Now let us contend with the senses themselves. “You tore me away,” he says, “from the womb.” What is torn away except what clings, what is fixed, what is fastened to that from which it is torn away so that it may be removed? If he did not cling to the womb, how was he torn away? If he who was torn away clung, how would he have clung except by being from the womb through that umbilical cord, like the channel of its own sac, attached to the origin of the womb? Even when something foreign is glued to something foreign, it is so made one in flesh and one in inward parts with that to which it is glued that, when it is torn away, it carries with it something from the body from which it is torn away, like a kind of sequel of the broken unity and of the channel of mutual union. Besides, what breasts of his mother does he name? Without doubt the ones from which he drank. Let midwives, doctors, and natural philosophers answer about the nature of breasts: do they not usually flow only when the womb undergoes its generative disturbance, the veins hanging from there drawing that residue of lower blood into the nipple and by that very transfer transforming it into the sweeter material of milk? That is why during the time of breastfeeding the monthly bloods are absent. But if the Word was made flesh from himself, not from sharing in the womb—the womb doing nothing, performing nothing, suffering nothing—how did the womb pour its fountain into the breasts, which it does not change except by having it? But it could not have blood to supply milk if it did not have the causes of that blood, namely the tearing away of its own flesh. What was new in Christ being born from the virgin is plain: only this, that he was from the virgin, according to the reasoning we have given, so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin.
orientation: Tertullian is answering heretics who say Christ was born 'through' or 'in' the virgin but not 'from' her, and he now argues from Scripture and physiology that Christ's flesh truly came from Mary's womb.

title: The Virgin's flesh must be Christ's own flesh
english: So if they insist that this was fitting for the newness of the thing—that just as the Word did not become flesh from a man's seed, so neither did he become flesh from the virgin's flesh—why should the whole newness not be this: that flesh not born from seed came forth from flesh? I will come still closer to the contest. “Behold,” he says, “the virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isaiah 7:14). What shall she conceive? The Word, certainly, not a man's seed—and certainly so that she might bear a son. For “she shall bear,” he says, “a son.” Therefore, just as it was hers to conceive, so what she bore is hers, even though what she conceived was not hers. On the other hand, if the Word became flesh from himself, then he conceived and bore himself, and the prophecy is void. For the virgin did not conceive and did not bear, if whatever she bore from the Word she conceived is not his flesh. But will only this voice of the prophet be made void? Or also the angel's announcement of the virgin's conception and birth? Or also all Scripture now, whatever proclaims the mother of Christ? For how is she his mother, unless because he was in her womb? But he received nothing from her womb that would make her a mother in whose womb he was. Flesh that is foreign does not deserve this name. No one calls it a mother's womb unless the flesh is a daughter of the womb. But it is not a daughter of the womb if it was born from itself. So Elizabeth too will be silent—she who was carrying the prophet, an infant already aware of his Lord, and who was moreover filled with the Holy Spirit. For she says without cause, “And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). If Mary was carrying in her womb not a son but a guest, Jesus, how does Elizabeth say, “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42)? What is this fruit of the womb, which did not sprout from the womb, which did not put down root in the womb, which does not belong to the one whose womb it is—and which is certainly the fruit of the womb, Christ? Or is it because he himself is the flower from the branch that came forth from the root of Jesse, and the root of Jesse is the family of David, the branch from the root is Mary from David, the flower from the branch is the son of Mary, who is called Jesus Christ—will he himself also be the fruit? For the flower is the fruit, because through the flower and from the flower every fruit is brought to ripeness into fruit. What then? Do they deny to the fruit its flower, and to the flower its branch, and to the branch its root, so that the root may not claim for itself through the branch the ownership of what is from the branch—the flower and the fruit? Since every step of descent is traced from the last back to the first, let them now know that the flesh of Christ clings not only to Mary, but to David through Mary, and to Jesse through David. Therefore God swears to him that this fruit from the loins of David—that is, from the posterity of his flesh—will sit on his throne (Psalm 132:11). If from the loins of David, how much more from the loins of Mary, through whom he was in the loins of David?
orientation: Tertullian is arguing against those who say the Word became flesh without taking flesh from the Virgin's womb, and he now presses the testimony of Isaiah and Elizabeth to show that Mary was truly Christ's mother.

title: Christ's flesh traced through the seed of David and Abraham
english: Let them then erase the testimonies of the demons that proclaim Jesus the Son of David, but they will not be able to erase the testimonies of the apostles, if the demons' testimonies are unworthy. Matthew himself first of all, the most faithful commentator on the gospel, as the Lord's companion, began for no other reason than to make us sharers in the carnal origin of Christ: "The book of the birth of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Since the order is traced step by step down to Christ's birth from these fountains of origin, with his lineage flowing on, what else is described but the very flesh of Abraham and David making a transmission of itself through each generation down to the virgin, bringing Christ in—indeed, Christ himself is brought forth from the virgin? But Paul too, as both disciple and teacher and witness of the same gospel, as apostle of that same Christ, confirms that Christ is from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3)—his own flesh, of course. Therefore Christ's flesh is from the seed of David. If it is from the seed of David according to Mary's flesh, then it is from Mary's flesh, since it is from David's seed. Whichever way you twist the saying, either what is from David's seed is from Mary's flesh, or what is from Mary's flesh is from David's seed. The same apostle settles this whole controversy by defining Christ himself as the seed of Abraham. Since he is Abraham's seed, much more is he David's, as the more recent. For unrolling the promise of blessing for the nations in Abraham's name—"And in your seed all nations will be blessed"—he says, "He did not say 'seeds,' as of many, but 'seed,' of one, which is Christ" (Galatians 3:16). We who read and believe these things, what quality of flesh ought we—and can we—recognize in Christ? Certainly none other than Abraham's, since Christ is the seed of Abraham; none other than Jesse's, since Christ is the flower from Jesse's root; none other than David's, since Christ is the fruit from David's loins; none other than Mary's, since Christ is from Mary's womb; and still further back, none other than Adam's, since Christ is the second Adam. It follows therefore that either they must maintain that those men had spiritual flesh, so that the same condition of substance may be traced down into Christ, or they must concede that Christ's flesh was not spiritual, since it is not reckoned from spiritual stock.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's flesh is ordinary human flesh because Scripture traces his descent through Mary from David, Abraham, Jesse, and Adam.

title: The Sign of the Virgin Birth
english: But we recognize that the prophetic voice of Simeon, pronounced over the Lord while he was still a newborn infant, is being fulfilled: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be contradicted" (Luke 2:34). For the sign of Christ's birth, according to Isaiah, is this: "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son" (Isaiah 7:14). So we recognize the contradictable sign: the conception and childbearing of the virgin Mary. About this sign those Academics say, "She bore and did not bear, virgin and not virgin." As if, even if it had to be said that way, it would not be more fitting for us to say it. For she bore, because it was from her own flesh, and she did not bear, because it was not from a man's seed. And she was a virgin, as far as a man is concerned, and not a virgin, as far as giving birth is concerned. Not, however, in the sense that she therefore did not bear, and was therefore a virgin who was not a virgin, on the ground that she was not a mother from her own inward parts.

But among us nothing is doubtful, nor twisted into a two-edged defense. Light is light, and darkness is darkness, and yes is yes, and no is no; anything more than this is from evil (Matthew 5:37). She bore who bore; and if a virgin conceived, in her giving birth she married. For she married by the very law of the opened body, in which it made no difference whether the force of a male was admitted or emitted; that same sex unsealed it. This, in fact, is the womb on account of which it was also written of others: "Every male opening the womb will be called holy to the Lord" (Luke 2:23). Who is truly holy but the Son of God? Who properly opened the womb but he who opened it when it was closed? For in all other cases marriages open it. And so it was more opened, because it was more closed. Certainly she must be called not a virgin rather than a virgin, since by a kind of leap she became a mother before she was married.

And why should we argue further about this? It was with this reasoning that the apostle declared the Son of God was brought forth not from a virgin but from a woman, recognizing the marital event of the opened womb (Galatians 4:4). We do read in Ezekiel about that cow which bore and did not bear. But see whether the Holy Spirit, already foreseeing you, has not marked you with this saying, as people who would dispute about the womb of Mary. Otherwise he would not have spoken doubtfully against his own simplicity, when Isaiah says, "She will conceive and bear."
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's flesh was truly born of Mary, and here he interprets Simeon's prophecy and Isaiah's sign to show that the virgin conception and birth are the very sign that will be contradicted.

title: The same Christ in the same flesh
english: Isaiah hurls a reproach against the heretics themselves, and first of all he says, “Woe to those who make sweet bitter and darkness light” (Isaiah 5:20). He marks those who do not keep these terms in the light of their own proper meanings: so that soul is nothing other than what is called soul, and flesh is nothing other than what is seen, and God is no other than the one who is proclaimed.

Therefore, foreseeing Marcion, he says, “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isaiah 45:5). And when elsewhere he says the same thing in the same way, “Before me there was no God” (Isaiah 43:10), he strikes at those genealogies of Aeons of the Valentinians, whatever they are. And “He was born not from blood nor from the will of the flesh and of a man, but from God” (John 1:13) answers Ebion.

Likewise, “Even if an angel from heaven should evangelize to you otherwise than we do, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1:8) is aimed at the energema, the son of the Apellean virgin Philumene. Certainly, “He who denies that Christ has come in the flesh, this one is antichrist” (1 John 4:2-3). By pronouncing the flesh naked and absolute and by the simple name of its own nature, he strikes down all who dispute about it.

So too, by defining that Christ himself is one, he shakes the arguers of a multiform Christ, who make one Christ and another Jesus, one who slipped away from the midst of the crowds and another who was detained, one who was radiant on a secluded mountain in the encircling cloud under three witnesses, another who was passive and ignoble among the rest, one who was courageous, another who trembled, and finally one who suffered and another who was raised. Through this they also assert their own resurrection in another flesh.

But it is well that the same one who suffered will come from the heavens, and the same one who was raised will appear to all. And they will see and recognize him, those who pierced him, surely the very flesh against which they raged, without which he could neither exist nor be recognized. So let those blush who assert that the flesh sits in the heavens empty of sense as a sheath with Christ drawn out, or who say that flesh and soul are equal, or that it is only soul, and no longer flesh.
orientation: Tertullian is closing his proof that Christ's flesh was true human flesh born of the Virgin, and now turns Scripture against all who divide or deny that flesh.

title: Closing summary of the proof of Christ's flesh
english: But enough has been said on the present subject. I think the proof has now been sufficiently established that the flesh in Christ was both born of the virgin and human. This proof alone, once discussed, could have sufficed, apart from the clash with each of the diverse opinions, which we have provoked over and above what was needed with their arguments and the Scriptures they use, so that by what we have proved—what the flesh of Christ was and whence it was, what it was not—we have decided in advance against all of them. But so that the resurrection of our flesh, which must be defended in another little book, may form the conclusion of this common preface, it will have here its preliminary construction, since it is now manifest what sort of thing that was which rose again in Christ.
orientation: Tertullian is concluding his argument that Christ's flesh was truly born of the Virgin and truly human, and he is preparing to hand over the topic of the resurrection of our flesh to another treatise.
